problem: Hedge sharpened: source 'it may be apprehended that the national Government may in the end be stripped' became 'one may fear that ... will eventually lose'.
replacement: Now suppose the opposite arrangement, in which the provincial governments are given the power to regulate those same affairs of mixed interest. Society then leans the other way. The stronger force sits in the province rather than in the nation, and it is to be feared that the national government may in the end be stripped of the privileges it needs in order to exist.

problem: 'more peculiarly requires' became 'depends more than most governments', which adds a comparison with other governments that the source does not make.
replacement: The federal government is therefore, whatever precautions its founders took, so weak by nature that it particularly requires the free consent of the governed in order to survive. It is easy to see that its purpose is to help the States carry out, without difficulty, their resolve to stay united. As long as that resolve exists, its authority is great, moderate, and effective. The Constitution equips the government to control individuals and to overcome without trouble whatever obstacles they may try to put in its way. It was by no means established with the possible separation of one or more States from the Union in view.

problem: 'no standing armies to maintain, no taxes to levy' narrowed to 'no taxes to support them' (taxes tied to armies only).
replacement: Of the many reasons that make the existing Union useful to the Americans, two principal ones stand out to an observer. The Americans are, in a sense, alone on their continent, yet their trade makes them neighbors of every nation they deal with. Their isolation is only apparent. They need a certain degree of strength, and they can keep it only by staying united with one another. If the States were to split apart, they would not only reduce the strength they can now show toward foreign nations; they would soon create foreign powers on their own soil. Inland customs barriers would go up, imaginary boundary lines would cut across the valleys, territorial distinctions would restrict the courses of the rivers, and countless hindrances would keep the Americans from exploring the whole of the vast continent that Providence has given them to rule. For now they have no invasion to fear, and so they have no standing armies to maintain and no taxes to levy. If the Union dissolved, all these burdensome measures might soon be required. The Americans therefore have a very strong interest in keeping their Union. On the other hand, one can hardly find any material interest that would now tempt a part of the Union to break away from the rest.

problem: 'union and prosperity' rendered 'unity and prosperity' (Union term drift), and the purpose clause 'in order that they may continue to furnish' became a flat relative clause 'which keep supplying'.
replacement: The North carries the produce of the Anglo-Americans to every part of the world and brings the world’s produce back to the Union. It plainly has an interest in keeping the confederation as it now stands, so that the number of American producers and consumers stays as large as possible. The North is the most natural go-between linking the South and West of the Union with the rest of the world. It therefore has an interest in the union and prosperity of the South and West, so that they may keep supplying raw materials for its factories and cargoes for its ships.

problem: Hedge changed: 'he may perhaps be led to think' became 'He may even be led to think' ('perhaps' dropped, 'even' added).
replacement: An observer who examines the present condition of the United States by this principle will readily see that, although the citizens are divided into twenty-four distinct sovereignties, they still form a single people. He may perhaps be led to think that the Anglo-American Union is more truly a society than certain nations of Europe that live under the same laws and the same prince.

problem: Liberty/freedom drift: 'the liberty of the press' rendered 'freedom of the press' next to 'liberty and equality'.
replacement: The Anglo-Americans belong to several religious sects, yet they all look at religion in the same way. They do not always agree about which measures best serve good government, and they differ over some of the forms of government worth adopting. But they are unanimous about the general principles that should govern human society. From Maine to the Floridas, and from the Missouri to the Atlantic Ocean, the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. Everywhere the same ideas are held about liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, trial by jury, and the responsibility of the agents of government.

problem: 'The probable unanimity of the States is diminished as their number increases' sharpened to 'the chance that they will agree on anything shrinks'.
replacement: The weaker each party to a contract is individually, the better the chances that the contract will last, since their safety then depends on staying united. In 1790 the most populous of the American republics had fewer than 500,000 inhabitants. *g Each felt how insignificant it was as an independent people, and that feeling made it easier to comply with the federal authority. But consider a confederate State like New York, which counts 2,000,000 inhabitants and covers a territory equal to a quarter of France. *h Such a State feels its own strength. It may keep supporting the Union because the Union helps its prosperity, but it no longer sees the Union as necessary to its existence. And while it remains a party to the federal compact, it soon aims at preponderance in the federal assemblies. The likelihood of unanimity among the States diminishes as their number grows. Today the interests of the different parts of the Union do not conflict. But who can foresee the many changes still to come in a country where towns are founded from one day to the next, and States almost from one year to the next?
